newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FORECAST - Israel's May CPI seen up 0.7-0.9 percent.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Israel's May CPI seen up 0.7-0.9 percent.

text.p: Israel's May consumer price index (CPI), to be released on Sunday, is expected to show a rise of 0.7 to 0.9 percent against an increase of 0.7 percent in April, economists forecast.
In May 1996 the index climbed a steep 1.7 percent as housing prices, an important component in the index, shot up 3.6 percent.
A rise of 0.9 percent would bring year-on-year inflation to 8.5 percent. The government has set an inflation target of 7-10 percent for all of 1997.
First International Bank of Israel is looking for an 0.7 percent increase in the May CPI, with housing prices rising about the same level.
"An 0.7 percent rise in the CPI is below average for the month," the bank's chief economist Hezy Gutman said.
Bank Hapoalim is forecasting a CPI rise of 0.8 percent while Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets, is estimating an increase of 0.9 percent.
"In May basically there was a continuation of seasonal factors from April," Katz said.
He estimated clothing prices increased four percent while fruit and vegetable prices gained four to five percent as summer fresh produce entered the market.

"The Central Bureau of Statistics measures the prices of produce as it enters the market in comparison to prices last year when it left the market, so the prices of items like watermelon and peaches are relatively high," Katz said.
Bank Hapoalim is forecasting inflation for all of 1997 will total nine percent against 10.6 percent in 1996.
Gutman said a rise of about 0.7 percent in the CPI would set the stage for a cut in interest rates later this month when the Bank of Israel announces its July monetary programme.
"The CPIs have been low, the budget data have been surprisingly good, unemployment is rising and wages are stable," Gutman said.
M1 money supply is estimated to have been unchanged in May, he added.
One factor that could cause some inflationary concern is the soaring Tel Aviv stock market, which could lead to an expansion in money supply, Gutman said.

Katz said one reason stock prices have risen so sharply is expectations that the central bank will lower rates as part of a wider economic programme that could include widening the trading band in which the shekel can fluctuate against the basket of foreign currencies.
Katz said he believes the central bank will either leave its key lending rate unchanged or lower it by a symbolic 0.3 percentage point.
Last month the central bank left the rate unchanged at an annualised 13.9 percent.
- Tova Cohen, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x238 TCC DER
